1.sense: An oath by animals at a gallop, and the second word is the noise their breathing makes. The surah starts at full speed and does not slow down for five verses.

notes.t: What the ʿadiyat are is an old disagreement. Ibn ʿAbbas is reported to have read them as horses in a raid, and a report from ʿAli reads them as the camels of the pilgrims running from ʿArafat down to Muzdalifah. The two readings put the surah in two different settings, one military and one at Hajj.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the difference between the two positions and the later exegetes divided over it

notes.t: Dabh is the sound made by a horse's breath when it is running past the point of comfort. Arabic keeps a separate word for it, so the oath is sworn by animals that are spending themselves, not by animals standing in a field.

Five verses of oath come before anything is sworn to, and every one of them is about motion. Nothing is claimed until verse six, and by then the reader has been given noise, sparks, dust and a collision.

links.why: another surah opening on a run of oaths by things in violent motion
tethered horses named as something a community keeps ready

words.g: and those that strike out fire

2.sense: Hooves on stone at speed throw sparks. The detail places the running in the dark, or at least before there is enough light to see by, which sets up the next line.

notes.t: Muriyat is the participle of the verb for drawing fire out of something that did not look as though it had any, the verb used of a fire drill and of striking flint.
The Qur'an uses the same root of the fire people bring out of green trees, which is its standing example of fire hidden inside something wet.
Fa, and then, joins each oath to the one before it. The five lines are one continuous action broken into stages rather than five separate things being sworn by.

links.why: the fire you strike, put as a question about who made it
fire brought out of the green tree, the same root and the same argument

3.sense: The hour is given without being explained. Raids were made at dawn, when a camp is still asleep and there is just enough light to ride by, and the first audience did not need that spelled out.

notes.t: Ighara is the technical word for a raid, a fast strike on a settlement rather than a battle between two lines. It tells you the size of the force and how long the whole thing lasted.
Morning is the Qur'an's recurring hour for a people being overtaken, and one verse asks flatly whether the morning is not near.
Three lines in a row end on the same sound, dabhan, qadhan, subhan, and each is a single word placed after the participle. The rhyme is doing the pacing.

links.why: their appointed time is the morning, and is the morning not near
a punishment that came upon them early in the morning

4.sense: Dust goes up. The verb changes from a participle to a finite past tense with a feminine plural ending, so the description stops circling and lands on something that happened at a moment.

notes.t: Naqʿ is dust that has been lifted and is hanging in the air. From a distance it is the first thing visible of a raid, before any rider can be made out, and the surah gives it in that order.

The pronoun in bihi, with it or in it, has no stated antecedent. Exegetes have referred it to the place raided, to the hour, and to the running itself, and none of the three changes what is being described.
notes.src: at-Tabari and the later commentators offer several referents for the pronoun

notes.t: The shift from participles to a verb is where the scene stops being a description of a kind of animal and becomes an event with a time attached to it.

links.why: an earlier people who turned over the earth, the same verb of stirring up
mountains reduced to dust hanging in the air

words.g: and they drive into the middle of

5.sense: The horses arrive at the centre. Nothing is said about an approach, because this is where the raid ends, with the riders already inside the crowd rather than closing on it.

notes.t: Wasata means to reach the middle of a thing, not to pass through it. The verse leaves them there and says nothing about the outcome, which is not the subject.
Jamʿ is a gathered body of people. Read as a raid it is the enemy host, and on the reading that the ʿadiyat are the camels of pilgrims it is Muzdalifah, which is itself called Jamʿ in Arabic.
notes.src: the two senses follow the two positions on verse one, both recorded by at-Tabari

notes.t: Five oaths have now been sworn and nothing has been sworn to. Everything so far has been noise and movement, and the point of it arrives in the next line without any transition.

links.why: the massed body defeated and turning its backs, the same word for a host
two forces meeting, given as a sign to look at

6.sense: This is what the five oaths were for. The charge is laid against the species, not against a group, and it is about how a person stands towards the One who keeps him alive.

notes.t: Al-Hasan al-Basri is quoted explaining kanud as the man who counts up the hardships and forgets the favours. The word names a settled habit rather than an occasional lapse, which is why the verse can use it of everyone.
notes.src: quoted from al-Hasan al-Basri by Ibn Kathir in his commentary on this surah

notes.t: The lexicographers say a stretch of ground is called kanud when it gives nothing back after rain. Applied to a person the picture is of something watered that produces nothing.

The oath and the charge are joined by a contrast the surah never states. Horses spend themselves completely for a rider who feeds them, and the animal does it without being told twice. The claim about man follows immediately.

links.why: man delighted by mercy and denying as soon as harm reaches him
man called deeply unjust and ungrateful right after a list of what he was given

7.sense: Somebody can testify to the ingratitude of the previous verse. The Arabic does not say outright who, and the sentence works whether the witness is the man or his Lord.

notes.t: The exegetes are divided on the pronoun. Read one way the man himself is the witness, so he knows what he is and could be put on the stand about it. Read the other way the witness is Allah, so the One he is ungrateful to is also the One who saw it. Both readings are early.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both, and both are held by later commentators

notes.t: On the first reading the verse takes away the defence of not having known. Ingratitude here is not something done in the dark by accident, it is done by somebody who could describe it if asked.
The Qur'an says elsewhere that a man sees clearly against himself even while he is putting his excuses forward, which is the same idea stated at length.

links.why: a man is evidence against himself no matter what he offers
the day tongues and hands and feet testify about what was done

8.sense: The third statement about the same man. He is strong at one thing, and what he is strong at is wanting more. The surah puts it directly after saying he knows what he is.

notes.t: Khayr here means wealth rather than good. The Qur'an uses the word this way in the verse on bequests, where a man is said to leave khayr behind him, and property is what is meant.
Shadid is the word for physical strength and hardness. Using it of an attachment says that this is where the man's force actually goes, whatever else he says he cares about.
The three statements run in a deliberate order. He is ungrateful, he knows it, and he is fully occupied with something else. The third explains how the first two sit together without discomfort.

links.why: you love wealth with a love that leaves no room
piling up more kept you busy until you reached the graves

9.sense: The question turns on knowing rather than believing. What is buried is not released, it is emptied out, the way a container is tipped over.

notes.t: Buʿthira is used of upending a vessel and of digging ground up and turning it over. The graves in this image are not opened from the inside; the contents are put out.
Surah al-Infitar uses the same verb of the same subject, and puts it in a list with the sky splitting and the seas breaking open.

The verse asks does he not know, not does he not believe. It treats the resurrection as something the man already has enough in hand to work out, and the failure as one of attention rather than information.

links.why: the same verb used of the graves in a list of that Day's events
coming out of the graves and hurrying towards their Lord

10.sense: The second container is opened in the line after the first. What was inside a person is not simply displayed; it is separated out from whatever it was mixed with.

notes.t: Hussila is the verb for getting the wanted thing free of what surrounded it, grain out of chaff or metal out of ore. It assumes the contents were not sitting there in a pure state.
Another surah names that Day as the day the secrets are put to the test, using a word for testing that separates the sound from the unsound.
The two verses are one movement. Bodies out of the ground and contents out of the chest, which are the only two places a person can put something away.

links.why: the day the hidden things are tested and shown
what is in the chests tested and what is in the hearts refined

11.sense: The surah ends on what He knows, not on what happens to them. Nothing is said about the punishment, only that the accounting will be done by someone the contents of a chest cannot surprise.

notes.t: Khabir is knowledge of the inside of a thing rather than the report of it. The verse does not say He finds out on that Day; naming the Day says when the knowledge is made to count against them.
The Qur'an puts the same point as a question elsewhere, asking whether the One who created would not know, and answering with two names, the Subtle and the Aware.
The surah opens with horses whose riders cannot be seen for the dust and closes with a Lord who reads what is inside a chest. The distance between the two ends is the argument it never states.

links.why: would the One who created not know, and He is the Aware
the same accounting given as the weight of a speck
